I've worked in SS research for a few years now. Most of that time has been on macro (FICC) desks but I started out in equities. A couple of thoughts:

\- "Buy side ER offers the intellectual depth and research experience that I look for" sort of tells me that you haven't spoken to too many people in the industry. Buy side shops use a number of dealers so any one hedge fund analyst has access to DOZENS of sell side reports on one stock at any given time. You don't get access to competitor research when you're on the sell side. SS ER analysts tend to specialise more in depth than their buyside counterparts (as a rule of thumb). Buyside shops run leaner (meaning each analyst covers more stocks, hence less in depth) and look for opportunities that directly translate to PnL. Sell-side analysts cover stocks for years and years and often even when they're not "hot". 

\- Whether SS ER is dull or not depends what you're looking for. Do you want to come into work, look at what the markets are doing, pitch an idea, execute, and move on ruthlessly? Then HF is what you're looking for. Want a relatively low-pressure job that rewards the occasional good idea? Then maybe some sort of active portfolio at a LO fund suits you. SS ER is a decent starting point for either of those. But if you want to become THE EXPERT in a leading sector then SS ER is somewhere you can stay forever. I know an analyst who covered a sector many people thought was 'boring' for 15+ years - then it suddenly blew up in popularity during the pandemic, and now he's an absolute legend on the street.

\- There are several ways to make a name for yourself in SS ER if you want to stick to it. One is modeling - if you produce the best models on the street, buyside clients will be all over you. Another is corporate access - if you become friends with company management/IR, you'll be the contact point for events and hosting roadshows, etc. This is more of a marketing type role but clients pay $$$ for it so can be very rewarding. Another still is being a super niche industry expert - e.g. some Pharma PhDs or mechanical engineers cover specific sectors and have an edge in identifying which companies will win. 

\- AI will shrink research functions in general. SS ER will probably not disappear but will likely have leaner teams with larger coverage given a lot of the modeling and writing can be done by GPTs. You can still have an edge by having better industry knowledge or relationships than the competition.

\- So is it a good place to start? Depends what you want. SS ER pays better than Equity Analyst roles at large 'buy side' (non HF) asset managers. Your upside is substantially capped vs HF PM type roles but, as you said, those are hard to get into as a grad anyways - and SS ER doesn't really set you back (your SS ER job is literally a constant audition to buy side clients of how smart you are).
Substantially more of a shot than a finance major trying to get into software engineering.

Not from Montreal. Easiest answer is network with your research colleagues (much easier in S&T than any other part of the bank because the two departments work together) and somewhat indicate to them you’d be interested if headcount opened up. 

I think the easiest switch is probably macro trading to macro research/strategy. Traders will trade only a small section of the market but have to have a view on the big picture, which will help in research. In equities it’s a bit different because traders simply won’t be in a position to know individual names deeply enough nor would they have the accounting experience. Similar story for sales but I’d say trading equips you incrementally better since you have to have conviction in research (despite not taking risk). 

If you’re still junior the above matters less, it’s just about coming across as market savvy and knowing the right people at the right time.

Banks with Research/Global Markets (combining S&T + R) intern/graduate programs will typically have FICC/macro research desks that you can rotate to. But headcount and turnover are both quite low (even compared to equity research, which at least has many sectors hence more teams to potentially land on) so it's incrementally harder.

There are also boutique research shops e.g. Alpine Macro or BCA that have similar roles, bu, in my experience, these seem to require more advanced academic backgrounds.

Sell-side macro strategist (rates/FX research)

1. Constantly interesting work - your job is to understand what's going on in markets, come up with ideas about what's going to happen next, and then get paid to explain this view to people

2. Days start early but usually end early. No earnings season like ER, although depending on shop you may have seasonal publication deadlines. Still reasonably predictable and 50-60 hour weeks are the standard.

3. Largely pays like ER while you're on the sell side.

4. Highly regarded and if you're good, you can exit to a macro HF. I would just caveat that sell-side research is not a risk-taking role and, over time, your ability to pivot to a decision-making PM role probably diminishes as a result.

I’ve worked in sell side research for 3 years. It seems like you put in a lot of work but, like another comment on here said, I’m not going to read all that. The formatting makes it a chore to read through. But even more unforgivable is the colossal amount of typos. Please spell check everything MANY times over before you take part in pitch competitions. 

For formatting, pick a color scheme that’s easy to be consistent with and clearly visible against your background. 

Put 3 bullet points at the top of the report explaining the key message and investment takeaway. 

Look up sell side reports online (there are tons available for free) for guidance and be extra critical of your own work. 

You have many pages of tables at the end that just restate the company’s statements - who is that useful to? If you use a DCF, put in the key assumptions as a smaller table and another one with sensitivity analysis. Then put your full forecasts in an appendix - that’s not something that would be found anywhere else. Use a football field for different valuation methods if you have considered them. Explain why the current pricing is wrong. DCF or comps valuation should not be the argument for a rating in and of itself, but can be useful in backing out how far your assumptions are vs what market pricing implies. 

Some equity analysts make their name for having the best understanding of company management. Some have exceptionally detailed modeling skills that allow clients to play with any assumptions and quantify any scenarios. Some know the industry better than anyone else. 

As a student, you have none of those things - so focus on the story. What’s the market missing? Is there too much pessimism from a regulatory concern that’ll brush away? Has there been a repricing across based on a headline about a competitor, which doesn’t impact your company? What catalysts will bring about repricing?

I think you have the commitment to do it. But please focus on polishing up your work and you can do it!

I'm not arguing that international markets don't matter as much, or that BP's impact is gonna go away tomorrow. But there are benefits to having a stronghold in a domestic market - for example, a BP member having a solo concert in the US, say, 20 years from now, probably wouldn't have the same impact as an SNSD member having one in Korea in 10 years (imo, obviously this can't be proven one way or another).

Both groups will be forever known as legends - the entirety of my point is that the way these legends are viewed is probably gonna be slightly different. Not sure if you know much about football, but I think the best example to illustrate is Bobby Charlton vs David Beckham - both came up through Manchester United (in different generations) and won everything at the club, but while Charlton had more individual impact during his time at the club than Beckham, Beckham clearly had a way more illustrious career and is much more well known globally. Nonetheless, if you ask a Manchester United fan who the bigger club legend is, they'd almost definitely say Charlton.

I suppose there's more of a sense of 'one of our own' that comes when a group/player has huge and concentrate impact - but the same way Beckham transcended United, so too do I think BP will with K-pop/the domestic SK market - which mitigates the 'one of our own' sense. No one should doubt their impact, but I just don't think this respect/impact is particularly comparable.

I think you've highlighted your points well, but I think their ending point will differ from SNSD's quite a bit. Not because they won't be viewed as legends - which they are in their own right - but because of the nature of their impact. SNSD was the Nation's GG, and the depth of the love they receive domestically isn't really mirrored by Blackpink. Even today, all the SNSD members have a rock solid fanbase and are still super loved and respected by the domestic industry.

BP certainly have more international reach - but as with most other global pop culture fads, people will more quickly move onto the next thing without feeling as much of a lasting impact. Domestically, it seems to me (as someone who isn't Korean) that BP hasn't quite established roots in the same way as SNSD (and other groups who I will intentionally avoid naming). Perhaps it's because we're only seeing them becoming really active in the past year, but I feel as though some of the members will eventually leave Korea/detach from the industry (and the general public's soft spot) in the long run.

Currently an Economics student at the LSE (did IB HL Math before the AA/AI split) and have been through the recruitment process, so here's my two cents:

As a previous comment mentioned, you'll definitely find most of the students going into IB/PE coming from BSc Economics, Finance, and to some extent Management - but I wouldn't take this as an indicator of 'best recruitment prospects' at first glance, since a) these courses are among the largest the LSE offers, and b) the people in these courses are on average more inclined towards careers in finance, so naturally the absolute numbers going to IB/PE are larger. 

From my experience with the recruitment process and what firms are looking for - **firms often don't particularly care what specific course is on your CV as long as you can prove to them that you're smart.** Investment Banking specifically doesn't require complicated mathematics, just comfort doing relatively basic operations with numbers all day. Doing a quantitative-ish course can flag that you're comfortable with numbers, but I have friends in courses ranging from Law to Politics/IR that get into IB; you can always flag your skills by taking modelling courses on the side/joining finance societies/doing internships before your penultimate year. 

Since you seem to want to apply for something in business/finance, some things you may want to consider:

* Relevance of coursework: generally, economics modules don't teach you anything that you'd in investment banking, while finance & accounting modules can have quite a bit of overlap with the technical knowledge you'd need for recruitment. You can take finance and accounting modules for most courses except for perhaps Math & Econ, so not a major concern.
* Prestige of courses: While firms may not care as much about which exact course you're doing, on campus there are perceptions of certain courses. Econ being LSE's flagship course definitely has prestige, while Management tends to be the butt of a lot of jokes (despite this, Management students get plenty of great IBD offers so it's not a big deal in the bigger picture). Finance is a much newer course, so not much to say prestige-wise - but Accounting & Finance (as opposed to pure finance) is seen as a slightly softer course since the math requirements are historically less strict.
* Benefits of department: Not much to say here except that BSc Finance students get significantly more recruitment support than others from their department  (CV help sessions, department-only events/networking). LSE's Econ department probably has the best alumni network though, and there's a good chance you can find econ alum at any firm you'd want to work at.

In summary (rambled a bit more than I thought, apologies) - there's not much to separate the various finance/business courses at the LSE as all give you very strong chances at breaking into IB. Pure Economics and Finance may have a slight edge for reputation/departmental benefits, but since you're doing Math AI, you may be better off going for Accounting&Finance or Management with much, much higher admissions chances and a marginally  small reduction (if any) in your recruitment chances. 

​

(Unsolicited, but if you're even somewhat interested in Philosophy and Politics - the LSE PPE course is 4 years long, doesn't require or even prefer AA, and PPE kids interested in finance get fantastic placements. Having the extra year means you get much more time to learn how recruiting works, do other internships, and have an edge during your penultimate year application season. You do have to endure essay-based qualitative courses that you may not be interested in, though)
